description: A grey-green subshrub that turns the stony hillsides violet in spring, shrubby moricandia is one of the most frequent plants of the Borj BouHedma relevés. Its glaucous leaves reflect the sun and its deep woody base survives both drought and grazing.

description: Schmitt's hammad is a compact, salt-excreting dwarf shrub of the stony steppe, as frequent as the broom hammad in the Borj BouHedma area. Its jointed stems store water and its small wind-pollinated flowers appear after the spring rain.

description: A succulent subshrub of the plateaux, mountain anabasis carries its leaves as tiny scales on fleshy jointed stems that store water. It thrives on the gypsum soils of the park's higher ground and is one of the most frequent species recorded around Borj BouHedma.

description: A woody, salt-loving subshrub of the hamada edges, salt gymnocarpos carries small fleshy leaves that store water through the long dry season. Livestock browse it, and the survey ranked it among the most frequent plants around Borj BouHedma.

description: Buffel grass grows in dense blue-green tussocks across the park's grazing plains and is one of the two most frequent species of the survey. Its bristly seed heads travel in the fur of passing animals, and the tussocks are prized fodder for flock and gazelle alike.

description: Alfa grass builds the open, pale-green tufts of the Bouhedma steppe: the esparto that has been cut for paper, cordage and basketry for centuries. It is the signature plant of the park's grasslands, the third most frequent species of the survey, and vulnerable on the Red List.

description: A low perennial grass whose knotted base gives it its name, nodose finger-grass spreads in the open ground between the shrubs of the park. Its finger-like spikes release seed through the hot months, and the young growth is grazed by livestock and by dorcas gazelles.

description: The small dorcas gazelle can live its whole life without drinking, taking moisture from leaves and green pods. It moves in pairs and family groups across the plain, always alert, and can sprint at 80 km/h to escape a closing golden wolf.

description: The common pipistrelle is the small bat of the park's open country, quartering the acacia stand and the edge of the steppe a few metres above the ground. In Bouhedma it was recorded from April to October and taken in the mist nets set across the water holes.

description: The meridional serotine replaced the northern serotine across North Africa, and it is the bat captured most often in Bouhedma — the largest catches of the survey. A powerful, deliberate flier, it feeds above the plain and the acacia forest and roosts in walls and rock fissures.

description: The maidenhair fern hides in the shadiest, wettest corners of Djebel Bouhedma, clinging to dripping limestone walls beside springs and seepages. Its fan-shaped leaflets on fine black stalks are unmistakable, and it dies back in summer to return with the first winter rains.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: Broomrapes are parasites with no chlorophyll at all — pale, scaly spikes that push up beside the roots of the plants they feed on. The tribe includes several species that attack crops and native shrubs across the drylands around the park.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: The Algerian rat snake is a large, alert climber of rocky slopes, drystone walls and farm buildings — the most snake-like predator of Bouhedma's ruins. Fast and harmless to people, it hunts rodents, birds and lizards, and will take eggs if it finds them.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: The Moorish gecko is the familiar wall gecko of North African courtyards, its tubercled skin and wide toe pads letting it cling to any surface. It hunts insects around lights after dusk and calls softly in spring to defend its stretch of wall.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: The Tunisian scorpion is the park's most widespread scorpion, sheltering by day under stones and in rodent burrows. Its sting is painful but rarely dangerous to a healthy adult, and it hunts beetles and other small invertebrates once the ground cools at night.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy
morphology_data: {"summary":[{"label":"Length","value":"6–9 cm"},{"label":"Colour","value":"Pale yellow-brown, matching the soil"},{"label":"Tail","value":"Robust, ridged, carried in an arch"},{"label":"Activity","value":"Nocturnal, sits at the burrow mouth"},{"label":"Diet","value":"Insects and other small arthropods"},{"label":"Habitat","value":"Stony ground, burrows, under rocks"}],"hotspots":[]}

description: The Saharan frog is the park's true water-specialist, living in the gueltas, springs and irrigation channels fed by the winter rains. Croaking males gather at the water from winter into spring, and the tadpoles must develop fast before the heat returns.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: An erebid moth of the park's dry scrub, Gnamptonyx innexa flies at night and rests by day among dry grass where its grey-brown wings make it almost invisible. Students recorded it during the park's night surveys.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: A striking erebid moth whose forewings carry bold black and cream bands over olive-brown, with metallic eyespots on the hindwings. It is a strong migrant, common across North Africa, and turns up in the park's light traps through the warm months.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: The beet armyworm is a small, restless moth known mainly as an agricultural pest, whose caterpillars strip the leaves of a wide range of crops and wild plants. The adults migrate in numbers and are regular visitors to the park's light traps.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: The praying mantis stands motionless among the park's tall herbs and shrubs, its spiked forelegs ready to snatch whatever passes. The foamy egg-case it glues to dry stems in autumn shelters the next generation through the cold months.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: Unlike its tree-dwelling relatives, this mantis hunts on bare ground, sprinting across sand and stone after small prey with surprising speed. Its flattened, sand-coloured body and shortened wings let it hide in plain sight on the desert pavement of the park's southern plain.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: Caddisflies are the park's quiet water-indicator: their aquatic larvae build cases of sand grains or plant debris in the springs and channels of Djebel Bouhedma, and the winged adults gather on the vegetation beside the water at dusk.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: The Saharan bluet is a small damselfly of North Africa's standing water, males flashing pale blue over black as they patrol the reeds. It breeds wherever water holds through the year, and is one of the region's characteristic odonates.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: The epaulet skimmer is a bold, sun-loving dragonfly of rocky desert streams, perching on warm stones and chasing rivals along the park's watercourses. Mature males turn powder-blue, and the pale 'epaulet' stripe on the thorax gives the species its name.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: The violet dropwing is one of the most vivid dragonflies of the Sahara's edges, males glowing violet-red as they perch on the tip of any dry twig above the water. It spreads north with the heat and is now common along Bouhedma's springs.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: This long-headed grasshopper is built for the park's dry grasslands: a pointed, cone-shaped head, a slender green or straw-coloured body and powerful hind legs for escaping over open ground. Its call is a faint crackling rattle carried on the wind.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: Ochrilidia is a genus of small, slender grasshoppers of the Saharan steppe, easily overlooked until they fly a short distance and settle again on bare ground. Like many desert grasshoppers they time their breeding to the right rains.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: Geotomini is a tribe of broad-winged, ground-dwelling grasshoppers of arid lands, recorded by the park's students on the stony plains of Bouhedma. Most identification stops at the tribe, since separating the genera needs close examination.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: Eugaster spinulosa is a heavy, slow bush-cricket of the North African scrub, its spiny hind legs and strong mandibles making it one of the more formidable plant-eating insects of the park. Males call from the ground through the warm months.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: The Barbary bush cricket lives on the ground among the low scrub of the Tunisian drylands, its long antennae and robust body typical of the barrel-bellied bush-crickets. It is active from spring into autumn and is a regular find on student surveys.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: The antlion's larva is the pit-digger of the park's sheltered sand: it buries itself in fine drifts, waits at the bottom of its conical trap and pulls down ants that stumble in. The adult is a delicate, lacewing-like flier of summer nights.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: Pimelia is a round, matte-black darkling beetle that walks the park's sands at dawn and dusk, its fused wing cases a shield against the dry air. Like many desert beetles it lives on wind-blown plant debris and whatever the desert provides.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: Phyllognathus excavatus is a small scarab beetle of sandy ground, one of the many dung beetles that keep the park's plains clean by burying livestock and wild herbivore droppings. Males carry a small horn on the head that gives the genus its name.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: The banded orb-weaver spins its wide, zigzag-streaked web low among grass and shrubs across the park, the silver-banded female far larger than the male. Grasshoppers and flies that blunder in are wrapped in silk and eaten at the web's centre.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: Leeches are recorded from the park's permanent waters, where they attach to frogs and water birds and move with looping, swimming strokes. Their presence shows how much life the small springs of Bouhedma support beyond the familiar headline species.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: The pale addax of the deep desert is recognised by its long, almost straight spiral horns and its white rump. Extinct in the wild across North Africa, it was brought back to Bouhedma, where captive herds are bred before being released onto the plain.
protection_note: Reintroduced in fenced grounds and released into open range; a sensitive species — the coordinates of sightings are never published.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: The golden jackal works the plain and the oueds alone or in pairs, feeding on insects, rodents, wild fruit and what the herds leave behind. Its wavering howl at dusk is one of the first sounds of the night in Bouhedma.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

nocturnal_activity: Crepuscular and nocturnal; the camera traps record it crossing the water points between midnight and dawn.

description: The caracal is the secretive cat of the rocky edges: a short red coat, black ear tufts and a look that disappears against the stone. It springs on hares and bustards from cover, so it needs scrub and silence more than open ground.
protection_note: Recorded from camera-trap images only; sightings are reported to the data manager.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

nocturnal_activity: Hunts alone after dark and rests in dense cover or a rock shelter through the day.

description: The ancestor of the domestic cat, slightly larger and longer-legged, with faint banding on the forelegs. It lives alone on the plain and in the acacia thickets, hunting rodents and gerbils at night.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

nocturnal_activity: Almost exclusively nocturnal, hunting along the burrow fields of the rodents.

description: A small, pale desert fox with very large ears that lose heat quickly. It keeps away from people, hunting insects and gerbils on the sand flats after dark and digging its burrow in open ground.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

nocturnal_activity: Leaves the burrow at dusk and is most active in the first half of the night.

description: The longest mongoose of the region: a dark grizzled animal with a black-tipped tail that hunts in pairs along the oueds and the reeds. It takes birds, snakes and eggs, and is rarely seen away from cover.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

nocturnal_activity: Feeds in the cool hours and rests in thick vegetation or a hollow log during the heat.

description: The genet is a slender, spotted climber, closer to a civet than to a cat. It slips through the acacia at night hunting insects and small birds, and rests by day in a hollow tree or a rock crevice.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

nocturnal_activity: Nocturnal and partly arboreal; it moves along the branches before coming down to the ground to hunt.

description: The largest rodent of the park, weighing up to 12 kg, with a crest of long bristles and black-and-white quills that reach 30 cm. It gnaws bones for minerals and spends the day in a burrow on the jebel.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

nocturnal_activity: Forages slowly at night, often in family groups, and always along the same runs.

description: A long-legged hare of the open steppe rather than a rabbit: it digs nothing but rests in a shallow scrape, and escapes at 60 km/h. Its young are born above ground, fully furred and ready to run.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

nocturnal_activity: Feeds at dusk through the night, crouching flat against the ground when disturbed.

description: A hopping desert rodent with a kangaroo's proportions — long hind legs, a tufted tail and almost invisible ears. It leaves star-shaped tracks around the bushes at night and never comes out in daylight.

nocturnal_activity: Digs a sealed burrow for the day and forages in short, saltatory dashes after dark.

description: A plump gerbil-like rodent of the saline soils that takes all its water from the succulent plants it eats. It digs its burrow at the foot of the halophytes and works the cool hours.

nocturnal_activity: Active in the cool parts of the day and stays underground through the midday heat.

description: The white-faced hedgehog of orchards and scrub, smaller than the European species, with ears that show above the spines. It walks long distances at night for beetles, snails and scorpions.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

nocturnal_activity: Travels up to a few kilometres in one night, bedding down under a bush or a wall at dawn.

description: A small, dark-faced hedgehog of the rocky desert with big ears and a bare-skinned flank line. It is most active after midnight, moving between shrubs and drinking at the water points the park keeps open.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

nocturnal_activity: Mainly active in the second half of the night; it will drink at the artificial water points in the dry season.

description: A small insect-eating bat of the cliffs and old walls whose nose-leaf ends in three points. It roosts in the cool caves of the jebel and hunts beetles and moths over the oueds after dusk.

nocturnal_activity: Leaves the roost in a loose swarm at dusk and hunts over water and vegetation.

description: A fast, long-winged bat of tomb walls and rock fissures, recognisable by the bare skin at the base of the tail. It hunts high above the plain in long straight passes.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

nocturnal_activity: Emerges early in the evening and feeds high in the open air, well above the plain.

description: A small pipistrelle of warm, dry country, gleaning insects from leaves close to walls, trees and rocks. It roosts in crevices and is taken in the nets set at the park's water points.

description: A bat of open country and short grass that flies high over the steppe after the last light. In Bouhedma it is recorded from spring to autumn, feeding on the small flies rising from the grazing grounds.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

nocturnal_activity: Feeds high above the ground, often over the water points, for several hours after sunset.

description: A big-eared bat with a deep slit down the face, flying low and slow across the plain to pick beetles and scorpions off the ground. It roosts in burrows and buildings and hangs in a distinctive head-down pose.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A medium-sized eagle of the cliffs, dark above and pale below with a dark leading edge to the wing. It hunts partridges and hares over the plain, and the pair stays on its territory all year.
protection_note: Nests on the cliffs of Djebel Bouhedma; nest sites are not published.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: The kestrel hangs motionless in the air over the road verges, tail fanned, watching for mice and lizards. It nests in a cliff niche or a cavity and can be seen hunting from first light.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: The largest owl of the park — ear tufts, orange eyes — hunting rats and hares from a rock or an acacia after dark. Its deep call carries over the plain on still nights.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

nocturnal_activity: Hunts from a perch after full dark and returns to the same rocky roost before sunrise.

description: A small, flat-headed owl that hunts by day as well as at dusk, perching on a stone or a post. It lives in the cavities of old walls and hunts beetles and mice on the bare ground.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

nocturnal_activity: Active from late afternoon through the night, often calling on warm evenings.

description: The partridge of the rocky slopes: grey head, black eye-stripe and chestnut flank bars. It runs uphill at the first alarm, and the covey gathers on the open patches at dusk.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A pigeon-like bird of the open sand, sandy above and warm orange below. The males carry water to the chicks in specially structured belly feathers, flying in to the water point every evening.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

nocturnal_activity: Drinks in the last hour of daylight; flocks gather at the water points on the plain.

description: The raven of the desert, larger than the hooded crow, with a bronze-brown neck and a heavy bill. It nests on the cliffs, follows the park's vehicles for scraps and watches the plain in pairs.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A streaked brown lark with a tall pointed crest, singing from a bush or a wire rather than in the air. It lives close to people and livestock and nests in a scrape under a stone.

description: The lark of the rocks and the cultivation edges, almost identical to the crested lark but with a shorter, squared crest and heavier streaking on the breast. Its song is shorter and less musical.

description: A plain, sand-coloured lark of the bare rocky hills, so close in tone to the ground that it is found first by movement. It sings from a low stone and keeps to the empty slopes.

description: A black wheatear with a white rump, hopping between the rocks and the old walls of the jebel. The male carries small stones to the nest hole as a display, and the pair defends a cliff territory all year.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A pale wheatear of the open sand; the male has a black throat and black ear-coverts. It hunts insects on the ground with short runs, tail cocked, and sings from a small bush after the heat.

description: A grey shrike with a black mask, perched on the topmost thorn of a bush. It impales beetles and lizards on the spines to hold them while it feeds — the habit that gives the family its name.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: The wild pigeon of cliffs and ruins from which the domestic pigeon descends: blue-grey with two black wing-bars. Feral flocks from the old farms also feed on the plain beside the wood pigeons.

description: The largest lizard of the park — up to a metre and a half — with a long forked tongue and a powerful tail. It digs out rodent burrows and takes eggs, and disappears down the sand at the first footstep.
protection_note: Protected by law and listed on CITES; sightings are photographed and reported, never handled.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A heavy, flattened lizard with a ring of hard spines on the tail, basking on the rock faces at midday. It feeds on the flowers and leaves of the desert shrubs and retreats into a deep burrow.
protection_note: Protected by law and listed on CITES; a sensitive species — the coordinates of sightings are never published.

description: The land tortoise of the scrub, with a high domed shell and a spur on each thigh. It grazes on herbs in the cool hours, shelters under a bush at midday and buries its eggs in the sandy soil.
protection_note: Protected by law and listed on CITES; sightings are reported to the data manager, the animal is not moved.

description: A slow, three-toed climber that catches insects with a tongue fired in a fraction of a second. It changes colour with light, temperature and mood, and the female buries her eggs in the sand of the plain.
protection_note: A protected species; it is photographed in place and left on its branch.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A heavy, boldly patterned viper of the low mountains and the cultivation edges, active from dusk to midnight. Its bite is medically important, so every encounter is reported to the park staff.
protection_note: Venomous and protected: rangers keep their distance and records are made from photographs.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

nocturnal_activity: Leaves its daytime shelter under a stone or a bush once the ground has cooled.

description: A very slender, fast snake of the sands, olive or striped, that hunts lizards in daylight. It freezes against a bush first, then leaves in a straight rush that is easy to lose in the grass.

description: A rock-dwelling agama whose males turn orange-red on the head during the breeding season. It basts on the stones of the jebel, waving its head to defend a territory of a few square metres.
